section.title: The Day of the LORD and Israel's Restoration
section.sectionRationale: The book turns from Edom to the whole world and from judgment to hope. The Day of the LORD is near for all the nations, the principle of recompense, as you have done it will be done to you, is stated, and then the vision opens onto Mount Zion delivered and holy, the house of Jacob restored and expanding, and a final word that gathers everything: the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
section.thesis: The Day of the LORD comes for all the nations on the principle of exact recompense; Edom is consumed, but Zion is delivered and holy, God's people are restored, and the whole vision resolves in the reign of the LORD Himself.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Day of the LORD and the law of recompense; the deliverance and enlargement of Jacob against Esau's stubble; the restored borders climaxing in deliverers on Zion and the kingdom of the LORD.

units.label: The Day of the LORD and recompense
units.note: as you have done, it will be done to you

verses.text: For the {{yomYHWH|Day of the LORD}} is near for all the nations. As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head.
For as you drank on My holy mountain, so all the nations will drink continually. They will drink and gulp it down; they will be as if they had never existed.

units.label: Deliverance for Zion, fire against Esau
units.note: holy, and the house of Jacob restored

verses.text: But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be {{qodesh|holy}}, and the house of Jacob will reclaim their possession.

Then the house of Jacob will be a blazing fire, and the house of Joseph a burning flame; but the house of Esau will be stubble; Jacob will set it ablaze and consume it. Therefore no survivor will remain from the house of Esau.” For the LORD has spoken.

units.label: Restored borders and the kingdom of the LORD

verses.text: Those from the Negev will possess the mountains of Esau; those from the foothills will possess the land of the Philistines. They will occupy the fields of Ephraim and Samaria, and Benjamin will possess Gilead.
And the exiles of this host of the Israelites will possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the exiles from Jerusalem who are in Sepharad will possess the cities of the Negev.
The {{moshiim|deliverers}} will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the {{meluchah|kingdom}} will belong to the LORD.

yomYHWH.gloss: The Day of the LORD, a recurring prophetic phrase for the appointed time when God acts decisively to judge the wicked and deliver His people. It is both a near historical reckoning and a picture of the final judgment. In Obadiah it widens the scope from Edom to all the nations and grounds the promise that wrong will be exactly repaid.

qodesh.gloss: Holiness, that which is set apart and sacred to God. Mount Zion, defiled when foreigners entered its gates, will be holy again, cleansed and consecrated as the LORD's own place. The word points beyond geography to a people and a city belonging wholly to God.

moshiim.gloss: Deliverers, saviours, those who rescue and set free, from the verb yasha, to save. The same root gives the names Joshua and Jesus, the LORD saves. In Obadiah the deliverers ascend Zion to rule, a role that finds its fullness in the one great Saviour, Jesus Christ.

meluchah.gloss: Kingship, kingdom, royal rule. The book's final word declares that the kingdom, the sovereign rule over all, belongs to the LORD. Every rival power, Edom and the nations included, gives way to the one true King, a hope fulfilled in the reign of Christ.

basic.context: The book now lifts its eyes from Edom to all the nations and from judgment to rescue. The Day of the LORD is coming, when everyone is repaid for what they have done. Edom and the nations are consumed, but Mount Zion is delivered and made holy, God's people are restored to their land and beyond, and the book ends with the greatest note of all: the kingdom belongs to the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophetic vision of God's future, mixing the near restoration of Israel with a picture of the final Day of the LORD. The rebuilt borders in verses 19 and 20 were partly fulfilled in history, but the sweep of the passage, all nations judged and God reigning, points beyond any single event to Christ's kingdom.
basic.originalLanguages: The Day of the LORD, yom YHWH, is the appointed time when God judges and saves. Zion will be holy, qodesh, set apart to God again. The deliverers, moshiim, come from the word to save, the same root as the name Jesus. And the last word, kingdom, meluchah, declares that the rule belongs to the LORD.
basic.typology: The delivered and holy Mount Zion points to the church and the heavenly Jerusalem. The deliverers who save and reign foreshadow Christ the great Deliverer, and the kingdom of the LORD is the reign He brings and shares with His people.
basic.christ: This passage points straight to Jesus. He is the true Deliverer who ascends Zion to reign; His name means the LORD saves. The Day of the LORD is fulfilled in His coming to judge and to save, and the final line, the kingdom will belong to the LORD, is realised in Christ's reign, now and at His return.
basic.god: We learn that God is perfectly just, repaying exactly what has been done, and perfectly faithful, delivering and restoring His people. Above all we learn that He is King; history is heading toward the moment when His rule is unrivalled and complete.
basic.crossReferences: Joel and Amos speak of the Day of the LORD and Zion restored. Revelation 11:15 echoes the last line, the kingdom of the world becomes the LORD's. Galatians 3:29 makes believers heirs of the promises to Jacob.
basic.oneStory: Obadiah ends where the whole Bible is heading: every wrong repaid, God's people delivered and holy, and the kingdom belonging to the LORD. That final line reaches its fulfilment in Christ, in whom God's reign comes and will one day fill everything.

context.literary:
Verse 15 is the hinge of the whole book. Up to this point every sentence has been aimed at Edom, in the second person, and the sentences of verses 10 to 14 were an accusation. At verse 15 the camera pulls back, the address widens from 'you' to 'all the nations', and the verdict arrives in a line that fits any court: 'As you have done, it will be done to you.' The word that carried the accusation, 'day', now carries the sentence. The day Edom would not leave alone is turned into the Day of the LORD.

The remaining verses fall into three movements. Verses 15 and 16 are a short, sharp judgment oracle about the cup. Verses 17 and 18 shift to a promise for Mount Zion and the house of Jacob, with the image of fire eating stubble. Verses 19 to 21 spread out into a map, naming regions in four directions and ending with a single sentence, 'the kingdom will belong to the LORD'. The prophet begins with a verdict and ends with a throne.

There are several devices at work. Notice the reversal of roles: Edom 'drank' in verse 16 as an act of revelry, and now the nations drink as an act of judgment. Edom 'cut off' in verse 14, and now Edom is 'cut off' by fire, verse 18. The refugees Edom hunted at the crossroads are answered in verse 17 by the word 'deliverance'. The people who were stripped of their possessions in verse 11 'reclaim their possession' in verse 17. And the whole movement is compressed into a single proportion: what was done is done back, and what was lost is returned. The book ends with an inclusio of sorts: it opened with a message sent among the nations against a proud kingdom, verse 1, and closes with a kingdom that belongs to the LORD.
context.historical:
The political world behind these verses is one of small nations living in the shadow of empires. The Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and took many of its people into exile. Edom, which had seemed to profit, did not outlast the century well. In later generations Arab tribes pressed into its territory, and the Edomites moved west into the southern hills of Judah, so that by the time of the New Testament the region was known as Idumea. Malachi 1:2-4, written when Judah was back in the land, already speaks of Edom's land as desolate and of its plans to rebuild as futile. Herod the Great, the king who ruled Judea when Jesus was born, came from an Idumean family, a reminder of how long the old story lingered.

The map in verses 19 and 20 is a map of a land that had been lost. The Negev is the dry south, and the 'foothills' are the Shephelah, the low country between the mountains and the coast, as the footnote to verse 19 says. Ephraim and Samaria are the old northern heartland, and Gilead lies east of the Jordan. The exiles of Israel, the northern kingdom taken away by Assyria, and the exiles of Jerusalem, carried off by Babylon, are both mentioned. Zarephath is a Phoenician town near Sidon, 1 Kings 17:9, which marks the northern edge. Sepharad is a place the Bible mentions nowhere else, and its location is uncertain; later Jewish tradition used the name for Spain, which is why we speak of Sephardic Jews.

The promise that 'the house of Joseph' will join 'the house of Jacob' as a flame speaks to the division of the kingdom after Solomon. For a people broken into north and south and scattered, the prospect of one people returning to all its land was a public hope, the same hope Ezekiel 37:21-22 gives in the picture of two sticks made one.
context.canonical:
The Day of the LORD is one of the most important phrases in the Prophets, and Obadiah is among the earliest to use it. Joel 1:15 says 'the Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty'; Isaiah 13:6 and Zephaniah 1:14-15 echo the cry, and Zephaniah piles up the terms: wrath, trouble, distress, darkness. In each case the Day is both terrifying and a rescue, a day when God sets the world right. Joel 2:32 and Obadiah 17 share the line about deliverance on Mount Zion, and Joel 3:4 and 3:7 use the very promise of Obadiah 15, 'I will return your recompense upon your heads'. Peter will quote Joel 2:32 on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:21.

The cup in verse 16 is its own thread. Jeremiah 25:15-17 is told to take 'this cup of the wine of wrath' and make the nations drink; Habakkuk 2:16 says 'the cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you'; Psalm 75:8 and Isaiah 51:17 speak of the same cup. Jeremiah 49:12 says to Edom: 'you must drink it too'. The thread runs through to Revelation 14:10 and 18:6. At Gethsemane Jesus prays that this cup might pass from Him, Matthew 26:39, and at the Last Supper He gives a different cup, 'My blood of the covenant', Matthew 26:27-28.

The last verse resonates widely. 'Dominion belongs to the LORD', Psalm 22:28; His kingdom 'will never be destroyed', Daniel 2:44; 'the LORD will become King over all the earth', Zechariah 14:9. The New Testament picks the line up in Revelation 11:15, and Gabriel's promise to Mary that Jesus will 'reign over the house of Jacob forever', Luke 1:33, uses the same house of Jacob as Obadiah 17 and 18. Amos 9:12 closes the circle by speaking of the 'remnant of Edom' possessed by a restored Israel, quoted at the Jerusalem council in Acts 15:16-17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Obadiah's closing verses were meant to turn the eyes of a defeated people upward. The earlier verses told them that Edom's crime was seen; these verses tell them what happens next. They are written to people tempted to read the fall of Jerusalem as the end of God's purposes, and they insist the opposite: the Day is not over, it is still to come, and it will land on those who thought they had escaped it.

The prophet means to teach three things. The first is the principle of recompense, which he states in the first-person plural of all history: whatever you do will return. That is meant both as comfort to the oppressed and as warning to the proud. The second is the promise of a remnant, that Mount Zion will be a place of deliverance and holiness, so that survival is not an accident but a gift. The third, and the one the book is built to reach, is that God is King. The map of conquered territories in verses 19 and 20 is a way of saying the earth belongs to Him, region by region.

His hearers were meant to respond in patience and hope. They are not to repay Edom themselves; they are to trust that the repayment is set, and to live as people who expect the kingdom.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is prophecy, so it describes what God will do and does not command what Israel must do. Nothing here is a call for the people of God to take land by force or to destroy a neighbouring people. The images of fire among stubble and of ascending Zion to rule are given as a promise that God Himself will carry out.

The lines that remain as direct instruction are the ones the rest of Scripture carries over. 'As you have done, it will be done to you' is not a mandate for revenge but a statement of how moral order works, and Scripture treats it as a reason for fairness, Matthew 7:2 and Galatians 6:7. The vision of Zion made holy is a call to be holy, Leviticus 19:2. And the closing line is a standing call to worship. Care is needed with the geographical promises: the New Testament does not read them as a deed to be enforced by Christians in any political programme, and it understands the inheritance in terms of Christ, Galatians 3:29.

debates.question: Who is the 'you' that drank on God's holy mountain in verse 16?

views.label: Judah, who drank the cup of wrath on Zion
views.case: The holy mountain is Zion, and Judah suffered God's judgment there in 586 BC. On this reading the verse says: as you, My people, drank My cup on My holy mountain, so all the nations will drink it too. The thread of Jeremiah 25:15-29, where the cup goes first to Jerusalem and then to the nations, supports it, and so does Jeremiah 49:12, 'if those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished?'

views.label: Edom and the nations, who drank in celebration
views.case: Edom is the 'you' of every verse before this, and the feast of looters on the ruins of Zion fits the carousing of verse 16. The cup then belongs to the revellers: those who drank in triumph on God's mountain will drink in ruin. The weakness is that the 'you' shifts from singular to plural, which suggests a change of addressee.

debates.bearing: The two readings differ in who first holds the cup, but they agree on its sequence: judgment begins with God's people and goes out to the nations, a pattern Peter states in 1 Peter 4:17. Either way the cup of wrath is real, and Christ drinks it for His own, Matthew 26:39.

debates.question: How is the restoration and the kingdom of the LORD fulfilled?

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ and His kingdom
views.case: The New Testament sees the promises to Jacob realised in Christ and His people, the true Zion and heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22, with the reign of the LORD inaugurated at Christ's first coming and consummated at His return, Revelation 11:15. Acts 15:16-17 reads the rebuilt tent and the possession of Edom's remnant as the gathering of the Gentiles.

views.label: A future national restoration of Israel
views.case: Some read the repossessed borders and the rule over Esau's mountains as awaiting a literal, future restoration of national Israel in the land, with these promises fulfilled in a coming age.

views.label: Partly fulfilled in the return and later history
views.case: A third group sees a first stage in the return from exile and the later expansion of Judean power into the old territory of Edom, with the full meaning still ahead. On this reading the passage works on two levels, a near fulfilment that is real and a final one that is larger.

debates.bearing: Whatever the shape of fulfilment, the last line settles everything: the kingdom belongs to the LORD, secured in Christ.

debates.question: Does 'no survivor will remain from the house of Esau' mean Edom is wiped out entirely?

views.label: A total end of the nation as such
views.case: Verse 18 is a flat statement, and the history bears it out in that Edom disappears as a nation. The language of stubble consumed by fire is final.

views.label: Judgment on the system that opposed God, with a remnant for mercy
views.case: Amos 9:12 speaks of Israel possessing 'the remnant of Edom' and 'all the nations that bear My name', so a remnant is envisaged. The total language is the prophets' regular way of describing the end of a power, not of every person.

debates.bearing: Both agree the pride and hostility of Edom end. The wider canon keeps a door open for individuals from every nation to be gathered into Zion, as James reads Amos in Acts 15:17.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 15 is built on a single Hebrew noun, gemul, 'recompense', a word for what is dealt back to someone. It is the word Joel 3:4 and 3:7 use for the very thing God says He will return 'upon your heads', and it is built from the same family of words as the verb for weaning and for rendering a deed. The phrase 'upon your own head' is an idiom for consequences that fall back on the one who caused them. The sentence 'As you have done, it will be done to you' is a perfect statement of lex talionis, but it is delivered not as human law but as a description of how God's order works.

The verb of verse 16, 'drink', is the key to the picture. Drinking is used in the prophets for receiving what God hands out, and the vessel is the cup. The final clause says the nations will drink until they are 'as if they had never existed', a Hebrew idiom of complete disappearance. The BSB's pair 'drink and gulp it down' sounds like the heavy swallowing of a drunkard, which is part of the point: the nations take the cup eagerly, not knowing what is in it.

In verse 17 the word for 'deliverance', peletah, shares its root with the 'fugitives' of verse 14, pelitav. Edom stood at the crossroads to cut off the pelitim, the escapees; God answers that on Zion there will be peletah, the escape itself. A single root has been turned from a trap into a refuge. The word 'reclaim' translates the Hebrew verb yarash, 'to take possession, inherit', which is the same verb that governs the whole list of territories in verses 19 and 20. The land lost in verse 11 is repossessed through the verb of inheritance. Joel 2:32 uses the same noun for deliverance on the same mountain.

Verse 18 pictures the house of Jacob as fire and the house of Joseph as a flame, and Esau as stubble, qash, the dry straw that burns instantly. The image is familiar from Exodus 15:7, where God's wrath 'consumed them like stubble'. Joseph is named alongside Jacob to include the northern tribes, descended from Joseph's sons, as Ezekiel 37:21-22 hopes for the reunion of north and south.

The last verse has a textual wrinkle. The BSB footnote reports that the Hebrew has 'The deliverers will go up' while the Septuagint reads 'Those being delivered will go up'. The Hebrew word is the plural of moshia, the title borne by Othniel, 'a deliverer to save them', Judges 3:9, and used for the saviours God raised in Nehemiah 9:27. The verb translated 'rule' is the ordinary verb to judge, shaphat, so these deliverers come up Zion to judge Esau's mountain, the way the judges of Israel's early history did, by delivering and then governing.

typology.type: The cup of wrath in verse 16
typology.fulfillment: The cup that all nations must drink reaches its climax in Gethsemane, where Jesus asks that 'this cup' pass from Him, Matthew 26:39, and in His words from the cross. Where Obadiah's nations drink to the dregs, Christ drinks the cup in their place, and then gives a different cup, 'My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many', Matthew 26:28. The type falls short in that the cup of Obadiah is only judgment, while the cup of the Supper holds judgment borne and forgiveness given.

Zion as the place where the escaped are safe becomes the church's identity. Hebrews says believers 'have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem', Hebrews 12:22. The correspondence is complete in status, but only partial in place: believers have come to it by faith and not yet by sight, and the city is still coming down, Revelation 21:2.

typology.type: The fire and the flame against the stubble
typology.fulfillment: A people through whom God's judgment burns. The picture is fulfilled not in a conquest by the church but in Christ, the one in whom 'our God is a consuming fire', Hebrews 12:29, and through His word, which will judge the last day, John 12:48. The type falls short because the church is called to bear witness rather than to execute the verdict; Jesus tells Peter to put his sword away, Matthew 26:52.

typology.type: The deliverers who ascend Zion to judge
typology.fulfillment: The judge-deliverers of Judges 3:9 are the pattern, and Christ the Son of David is the fulfilment, 'a Savior, who is Christ the Lord', Luke 2:11. The New Testament also says that His people will share in His judgment, 1 Corinthians 6:2 and Revelation 2:26-27. The limit is that the earlier deliverers rescued once and died, and each rescue needed another after it; this Deliverer rose from death and reigns forever, so that no further one is needed.

typology.type: The kingdom that belongs to the LORD
typology.fulfillment: The kingdom of God, announced by Jesus in Mark 1:15 as having come near, entering history in His person and promised at its end in Revelation 11:15. The type is not a shadow of something absent but the first light of something arriving, and its limit is time: the kingdom is already here in the Spirit and not yet fully here in the world.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by the shape of its hope, and the best way to see it is to follow its three great movements.

The first is judgment. 'As you have done, it will be done to you' sounds like terror to anyone who has done wrong, and the New Testament faces this squarely. Paul writes that God 'will repay each one according to his deeds', Romans 2:6. If that were the whole story there would be no hope for any of us. But the Gospels show what happens when the cup comes around. In Gethsemane Jesus prays, 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me', Matthew 26:39. The cup that Jeremiah and Habakkuk saw in the hand of the LORD is taken by the Son. He stands in the place of those who would have drunk it, and He drinks it until the dregs of the Day of the LORD have fallen on Him. That is why the New Testament can say there is no condemnation for those in Him, Romans 8:1.

The second is deliverance. Obadiah promises 'on Mount Zion there will be deliverance'. The Hebrew word for the deliverers, those who save, is the plural of the root behind the name Joshua and so behind Jesus, as the basic level notes. What the passage adds is the way the deliverer ascends. Christ goes up to Jerusalem, is lifted up, and rises, and from Zion He pours out salvation. Joel's line, 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved', is quoted by Peter at Pentecost, Acts 2:21, as the gospel's open door, and Hebrews says that believers have already come to 'Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem', Hebrews 12:22.

The third is the kingdom. Gabriel tells Mary of her son that 'He will reign over the house of Jacob forever', Luke 1:33, the very house of Jacob that Obadiah promised would be fire and flame. The consummation is described in 1 Corinthians 15:24-28, when Christ has put all His enemies under His feet and hands over the kingdom to the Father 'so that God may be all in all'. Edom stands in that picture for every power that sets itself against the King, and the last enemy that falls is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

Finally, the inclusion of Gentiles. Amos's promise that Israel will possess 'the remnant of Edom', read by James in Acts 15:16-17 as the Gentiles seeking the Lord, shows that the Deliverer's work reaches even the family of the old enemy. Christ takes the cup, ascends Zion, and brings Esau's children home. A caution: not every detail of the map in verses 19 and 20 is a coded picture of Jesus, and it is wise to let the New Testament's own use of the passage set the limits.
study.god:
This closing section shows God as judge, deliverer and king, and it holds these together in ways that are worth slowing down for.

He is the God of an ordered world. The line 'As you have done, it will be done to you' is not a threat invented for Edom but a statement of how the moral universe is built. God does not need to invent punishments; He lets deeds come back on the heads of those who did them, and He fixes the day. That is the root of the biblical idea that the world has a moral shape, in which pride falls, violence reaps violence, and the cup eventually comes round to everyone. The doctrine of divine justice here is not vindictive. It is exact and public, and it is stated in the name of a Judge who has already given warning.

He is the God who is jealous for His holy mountain. 'You drank on My holy mountain', He says, and the possessive matters. Zion is His, Judah is His people, and the offence against them is an offence against Him. The holiness of Zion in verse 17 is not first about human purity but about the presence of God; the place is holy because He is there, Psalm 99:9.

He is the God of faithful memory. The scattered exiles of the north and south are not forgotten. The list of regions, the Negev, the foothills, Ephraim, Samaria, Gilead, Zarephath, Sepharad, is a catalogue of everywhere God's people have been dispersed, and He knows each place. The same God who knew every crossroads where Edom stood knows every corner where the exiles sit.

And He is King. The book ends not with Israel but with the LORD: 'the kingdom will belong to the LORD'. Everything before it is a means to that sentence. This tells us what God is aiming at in history. His rescue of Zion is not the final purpose but the way His rule becomes visible.

Two tensions deserve honesty. One is the severity of verse 18, 'no survivor', against the mercy of Amos 9:12 and the Gentile hope of Acts 15; the Bible lets both stand, as Paul does when he speaks of the kindness and severity of God together, Romans 11:22. The other is the gap between promise and visible history. The exiles waited; the borders were never as wide as verses 19 and 20; and the kingdom is still being awaited. For worship this means praying as the church does, 'Your kingdom come', and receiving the kingdom as unshakable, Hebrews 12:28, with reverence and awe.

crossReferences.note: 'The Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.' Joel and Obadiah share the same phrase and the same sense of nearness. Joel's Day falls first on Judah and then on the nations, which helps explain why Obadiah moves from Edom's guilt to all the nations in one verse.

The LORD says to Tyre, Sidon and Philistia, 'I will swiftly and speedily return your recompense upon your heads.' It is almost word for word the line of Obadiah 15, applied to other nations, and it shows how the principle of recompense belonged to the prophets' shared vocabulary.

Jeremiah is told to take the cup of the wine of wrath and make all the nations drink from it. This is the fuller picture behind Obadiah 16: the cup is in God's hand, it goes round every nation, and nobody who is handed it can refuse.

'The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you.' The tyrant who made others drink to shame will drink to shame himself. It sets Obadiah's reversal inside a pattern: the one who stripped others of dignity is stripped of his own.

'On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has promised.' Obadiah 17 uses the same noun for the same mountain, so the two prophets confirm each other. Peter quotes the first half of this verse at Pentecost, so the promise opens onto the whole church.

God promises to gather the Israelites and make them one nation with one king, never again two kingdoms. It lines up with Obadiah's pairing of the house of Jacob with the house of Joseph, north and south joined as one fire against the stubble.

God raised up Othniel as 'a deliverer to save them'. The word for deliverer is the same one used of the deliverers in Obadiah 21, which tells the reader what kind of figure to expect: someone raised by God to save and then to govern.

The restored tent of David will 'possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name'. It softens the finality of Obadiah 18 without contradicting it, and it shows that the possession of Edom was, in God's plan, a gathering in as well as a victory.

James quotes Amos at the Jerusalem council to show that the Gentiles' inclusion was foretold. By giving 'the remnant of Edom' the sense of 'the remnant of men may seek the Lord', he reads Obadiah's closing hope as fulfilled in the church.

'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever.' The seventh trumpet gives Obadiah's last line its final form, with the Lord and His Christ now named together as the King.

study.oneStory:
Obadiah 15 to 21 is a compact picture of the whole Bible's end. The story of Scripture moves from creation to fall, to redemption, to new creation, and this passage lifts the last three into one frame.

It answers the fall. Since Genesis 3 and 4 the world has been a place where brother kills brother, where the proud are enthroned and the weak looted. The question under the whole Old Testament is whether that will stand. Obadiah's reply is no. There is a Day, and it is God's. The doctrine of the Day of the LORD is the Bible's insistence that history is not left to the strong, that every wrong is on record, and that the account will be settled. It is no accident that the word for the crime in verse 10 is the word for the violence of the flood generation: the Day answers the violence that began at the fall.

It sets up redemption. A remnant on Mount Zion, a house of Jacob made a fire, deliverers who ascend to judge: these are all promises that need a person to fulfil them. The Old Testament offered judges and kings, none of whom held. The New Testament names the One who does. The deliverer is Jesus, whose name is the name of the saving root; the Zion is the heavenly Jerusalem; the possession is the world that the meek will inherit, Matthew 5:5; the people are all who belong to Christ, 'Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise', Galatians 3:29. Strangers become 'fellow citizens with the saints', Ephesians 2:19, so that Edom's people, the old outsiders, can be gathered into the very house they once attacked.

It ends in new creation. The last verse of Obadiah and the last book of the Bible are bound by one sentence. In Revelation 11:15 the world's kingdom becomes the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ, and in Revelation 21 the nations walk by the light of the city and the kings bring their glory into it, 21:24. The mountain of the LORD, which Isaiah 2:2 and Micah 4:1-2 see raised above the hills with nations streaming to it, is the same Zion Obadiah saw. In that city the cup of wrath is gone, the crossroads are open, and no brother lies in wait.

Until then the church lives between the verdict and the throne. It does not take the cup into its own hands or the sword to the neighbour's door; it prays for the kingdom, bears witness, and waits, trusting that the last line of the shortest book in the Old Testament is also the first line of everything that comes after.

sermon.why: No sermon on Obadiah 1:15-21 from a trusted expositor could be confirmed by web search in this session, so none is listed.

quiz.q: What principle governs the Day of the LORD in verse 15?

options.text: Exact recompense: as you have done, it will be done to you.
options.note: Verse 15 states that one's own deeds return upon one's own head.

options.text: Unconditional mercy for every nation regardless of conduct.
options.note: Mercy is offered to God's people, but the Day here is one of just recompense.

options.text: Random calamity with no moral order.
options.note: The judgment is precisely measured to what was done, not random.

options.text: Reward based on national size and strength.
options.note: It is based on deeds, not on might; the mighty Edom is brought down.

quiz.q: What is the great note on which the book of Obadiah ends?

options.text: The kingdom will belong to the LORD.
options.note: Verse 21 closes with the LORD's unrivalled reign, the summit of the book.

options.text: Edom will finally be forgiven and restored.
options.note: Edom is consumed as stubble; the closing hope is the LORD's kingdom.

options.text: Israel will build a great army.
options.note: Israel is restored, but the climax is God's reign, not military might.

options.text: The nations will remain in power forever.
options.note: The opposite: every rival power gives way to the LORD's kingdom.

quiz.q: Who are the ‘deliverers’ who ascend Mount Zion, and to whom do they point?

options.text: Saviours, from the root yasha, to save; they foreshadow Christ, whose name means the LORD saves.
options.note: Moshiim shares the root that gives the name Jesus; He is the great Deliverer who reigns.

options.text: Foreign kings who conquer Zion.
options.note: They ascend to rule for God's people, not foreign conquerors.

options.text: Priests who offer sacrifices only.
options.note: Their role is to deliver and rule, pointing beyond priesthood to Christ the Saviour-King.

options.text: Angelic beings with no link to Christ.
options.note: The word means human saviours and points to Christ, not angels.

quiz.q: What happens to Mount Zion in the restoration?

options.text: There will be deliverance, it will be holy, and Jacob will reclaim its possession.
options.note: Verse 17 promises deliverance, holiness, and restored inheritance on Zion.

options.text: It will be abandoned and left in ruins.
options.note: The opposite: Zion is delivered and made holy again.

options.text: It will be handed over permanently to Edom.
options.note: Edom becomes stubble; Zion is delivered, not handed to Edom.

options.text: It will remain defiled as it was on the day it fell.
options.note: It was defiled, but the promise is that it will be holy once more.

quiz.q: How is Obadiah's closing hope fulfilled in the New Testament?

options.text: In Christ's reign, echoed in Revelation 11:15, the kingdom of the world becomes the LORD's and His Christ's.
options.note: The final line finds its fulfilment in the kingdom of God established in Christ.

options.text: In the rebuilding of Edom as a Christian nation.
options.note: Edom is consumed; the fulfilment is Christ's kingdom, not Edom's revival.

options.text: Only in a political state, with no link to Christ.
options.note: There may be a historical dimension, but the New Testament centres fulfilment on Christ's reign.

options.text: It is left entirely unfulfilled in the New Testament.
options.note: The New Testament takes up this hope directly in Christ's kingdom.

questions: The Day of the LORD repays each according to their deeds. How does the certainty that God will one day set every wrong right change the way you face injustice now?
Zion was defiled but promised to be holy again. Where do you long for God to cleanse and set apart something in your life that has been spoiled?
The deliverers point to Jesus, whose name means the LORD saves. What would it mean to trust Him more fully as your Deliverer this week?
The book ends with the kingdom belonging to the LORD. In what area are you still living as if the kingdom belonged to you, and how might you yield it to His reign?

God turned Edom's treachery back on its own head yet lifted His people to a restored and holy home. How does this move you to trust God with those who have wronged you rather than repaying them yourself?

translationNotes.note: As you drank on My holy mountain uses the image of the cup: Judah drank the cup of suffering when Jerusalem fell, and now all the nations must drink the cup of God's judgment continually until they are as if they had never existed.
For the LORD has spoken seals the certainty of the whole oracle.

The foothills renders a term the BSB footnote gives as the Shephelah or lowlands, the western foothills of Judea; the verse pictures God's people expanding in every direction into surrounding territories.

The deliverers will ascend renders a phrase the BSB footnote also gives as the deliverers will go up from, and the Septuagint as those being delivered will go up; the sense of saviours ascending Zion to rule stands in every reading, climaxing in the kingdom belonging to the LORD.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Obadiah 1:15-21. The BSB footnotes at verses 19 and 21 (Shephelah; the deliverers will go up from / LXX those being delivered) are reflected in the translation notes.
